wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: Compared with degraded sites, restored peatlands have lower carbon emission rates and over time can become net carbon sinks [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1]: restoration first cuts the emissions from degraded peat, and sequestration follows only later.
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: This row rests on a single institutional review, a Ramsar Convention briefing note on wetland restoration and climate resilience, citing earlier research rather than reporting its own measurements [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1]. It concerns peatlands only, gives no rates, and does not say how long the shift to a net sink takes.

wetland_management__fire__all.mechanism: The fire benefit runs through keeping peat wet. In the tropics, forested peat domes that were cleared, drained and replanted with palm oil plantations become vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years [ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1]. The evidence describes the harm that drainage does, which is the risk that rewetting peat is meant to reverse.
wetland_management__fire__all.conditionality: This row rests on a single institutional review, a Ramsar Convention briefing note on wetland restoration and climate resilience, which describes what draining tropical peat does rather than measuring fire after rewetting [ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1]. The statement is a citation of earlier work, gives no magnitude, and applies to peat domes, not to other wetland types or to farm-level fire risk.

wetland_management__flood__all.mechanism: Wetlands buffer communities from coastal storm surges, reduce wave damage and floods, and stabilise shorelines; the Ramsar briefing note presents this as a reason why wetland protection and restoration increase climate resilience as storms, flooding, droughts and heat waves become more frequent [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2].
wetland_management__flood__all.conditionality: This row rests on a single institutional review, a Ramsar Convention briefing note on wetland restoration and climate resilience, and the flood statement is one of its key messages rather than a measured result [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2]. It treats protection and restoration together, gives no magnitude, and does not say how quickly a restored wetland regains the buffering, at what flood size it stops working, or in which settings it applies.

wetland_management__heat_stress_hazard.mechanism: Wetlands cool the local climate by spending incoming energy on evaporation: in measurements at Trebon, Czech Republic, up to 60% to 70% of solar energy was transformed into sensible heat over a drained crop field against only 5% to 10% over an intact wetland, where 70% to 80% of heat is dissipated via evapotranspiration [ev_wet_microclimate_buffering_ramsar18_1].
wetland_management__heat_stress_hazard.conditionality: This row rests on a single institutional review, a Ramsar Convention briefing note on wetland restoration and climate resilience, which reproduces measurements from one temperate, high-income site [ev_wet_microclimate_buffering_ramsar18_1]. The comparison is between an intact wetland and a drained field, so it shows the target state of restoration rather than a measured gain at a restored site, and local cooling is a component of heat stress rather than a measure of heat stress on people, crops or livestock.

wetland_management__water_stress.mechanism: Wetlands store water from precipitation and slowly release it to the surrounding environment, which can also recharge groundwater aquifers and maintain atmospheric water cycles [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1].
wetland_management__water_stress.conditionality: This row rests on a single institutional review, a Ramsar Convention briefing note on wetland restoration and climate resilience; the unit is a general functional statement about wetlands, not a measurement of water availability after restoration [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. It gives no magnitude and does not address how much of the stored water reaches farmers.
